opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, at the time I don't think I weighed it as carefully as the question makes it sound. I was in high school in China, and applying to U.S. universities wasn't the standard path at my school. Most people were preparing for the gaokao, and there wasn't really an established pipeline or a counselor who knew the process well. So a lot of it was figuring things out myself: reading forums, looking up what the SAT and TOEFL required, trying to understand what a personal essay was even supposed to be.

The uncertainty was real. I didn't know if I was doing things right, and I didn't have anyone to benchmark against. But I think the motivation outweighed it, because I had this sense that the kind of education I wanted, more open, more exploratory, where you could follow your curiosity across fields, was more likely to be found there. I was already interested in computers and building things, and the U.S. seemed like the place where that kind of interest could really grow.

I also think there's a certain freedom in not knowing what you're doing. When there's no script, you're not comparing yourself to a script. You just try your best, and if it doesn't work out, you still have other options. For me the downside felt manageable and the upside felt huge. That asymmetry made the decision easier than it might look from the outside.

Looking back, doing it on my own taught me something that's carried through my whole career, including research: a lot of the most interesting paths don't come with a clear map. You learn to be comfortable making decisions with incomplete information, and you trust that you'll figure it out along the way.

r001.rationale: The response says his motivation for a more open, exploratory education outweighed the uncertainty, but it does not state that he wanted to avoid doing things he did not want to do.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't think I weighed it very carefully at the time, and that's probably why I did it. If I had sat down and done a proper risk analysis, I'm not sure I would have gone through with it.

I grew up in China, and when I decided I wanted to study in the U.S., there was already this whole industry around it: agents, consultants, people who would basically package you up and tell you which schools to apply to and what to write. My family didn't have the resources for that, and to be honest I was also a bit stubborn about it. I thought, if I'm going to go live in another country and study there, I should at least be able to figure out how to apply on my own.

So the uncertainty was real. I didn't know anyone who had done it this way. I was reading forums, piecing together what the SAT was, what a "common app" essay was supposed to sound like, whether my English was good enough. There was no feedback loop. You submit things and then you wait for months and have no idea if you did it right.

What kept me going was that the motivation was pretty concrete. I was already playing with programming and I wanted to be somewhere where I could build things and be around people doing research. That goal felt much more real than the fear of getting rejected. I think when the thing you want is specific enough, the uncertainty becomes something you just tolerate rather than something you solve.

And looking back, the process itself taught me something I use all the time now. In research, you're constantly doing things where nobody can tell you the right answer in advance. You read, you make your best guess, you commit, and you find out later. Applying on my own was my first real experience with that, and it made the later ones feel a lot less scary.

r001.rationale: The response says he wanted to apply on his own and that his goal of building things and doing research outweighed fear of rejection. It does not clearly state that avoiding things he did not want to do outweighed the uncertainty.

astra-6.text: I think the motivation made the uncertainty feel worth taking on. Preparing the applications independently meant I didn’t have a clear sense of whether I was doing everything right, and that was uncomfortable. But I wanted to give myself the chance to pursue that path. So I focused on the things I could control—figuring out the requirements, preparing the materials, and taking it one step at a time. I didn’t need to feel certain that it would work out before deciding to try.

r001.rationale: The response says the motivation to pursue the path made the uncertainty feel worthwhile, but does not state that Danfei Xu was motivated to avoid doing things he did not want to do.
